summary: Analyzes how protection and recovery for label switched paths work in multi-domain MPLS and GMPLS networks, where paths cross more than one domain. It looks at the schemes and processes already defined for setting up such paths, as described in a framework document, and examines how recovery fits them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a train route crosses several countries and a bridge fails, each railway must help fix it. This studies how backup paths work when a route goes through many separate networks.

subtitle: How to set up backup paths that don't share links or nodes across MPLS networks spanning multiple domains.

tldr.problem: MPLS networks span multiple domains (ASes, areas), and when a working path fails, a backup (recovery) path must exist that doesn't share the same failed resources. Computing such diverse paths across domains is complex because each domain may hide its internal topology.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes multiple schemes: management configuration, end-to-end path computation with visibility across domains, per-domain computation (sequentially or simultaneously), and cooperative computation between domains' path computers (PCEs).
tldr.outcome: Operators can choose the right combination of path computation and signaling for their security and scalability needs, with guidance on trade-offs between optimality and computational complexity.

facts.label: LSP types analyzed
facts.value: End-to-end recovery, 1+1 and 1:1 protection, shared mesh restoration

today: RFC 5298 is an Informational analysis document that remains relevant for operators designing multi-domain MPLS or GMPLS protection schemes. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Multi-Domain Recovery Challenge
sections.content:
MPLS and GMPLS networks use Label Switched Paths (LSPs) to route data. When a link or node fails, a recovery LSP provides an alternative path. The key requirement is that the recovery path must be diverse from the working path, meaning they don't share nodes, links, or shared-risk link groups (SRLGs) that could fail together.

In single-domain networks, one path computation point sees all the topology and can easily compute two diverse paths. In multi-domain networks (like when paths cross multiple Internet Service Providers or IGP areas), each domain may keep its topology private for business or security reasons.

The RFC analyzes how to establish diverse working and recovery LSPs when domains have limited visibility into each other's internals. It examines different trade-offs between computational complexity, optimality, and confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: A package might travel through Route A across three different delivery companies to get to its destination. If Route A breaks, you need a completely different Route B that doesn't rely on the same broken parts. Figuring out Route B is hard when you don't fully understand each company's internal routing.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC introduces three major design dimensions. Confidentiality: Networks can either expose full topology across domains (suitable for single operator or trusted environments) or hide internal details, revealing only boundary nodes and domain identifiers.

Path computation approach: (1) End-to-end: One central point (usually the head-end router or a Path Computation Element) sees all domains and computes both paths. (2) Per-domain: Each domain computes only its segment when the LSP reaches its boundary, expanding the path as signaling progresses. (3) Collaborative: Domain PCEs coordinate computation using protocols like Backward Recursive Path Computation (BRPC), combining per-domain privacy with multi-domain awareness.

Path computation timing: (1) Sequential: Compute the working path first, then compute a diverse recovery path afterward. Simpler but may miss solutions in complex topologies ("trap" scenarios). (2) Simultaneous: Compute both paths at the same time, considering diversity during computation. More likely to find solutions but requires more complex signaling mechanisms.

The RFC notes the fundamental tension: restricting information to individual domains (preserving confidentiality) may prevent optimal diverse path computation, but releasing full topology sacrifices business confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Three choices: Should each company see the others' secret routes? Should the head office plan both paths, or should each company plan just its own section? Should you plan the backup path at the same time as the main path, or plan it afterward?

sections.title: Schemes Without Full Confidentiality
sections.content:
When all domains are under one operator (such as a multi-area MPLS network within a single provider), domains can share complete topology. In this environment, three approaches work:

Management configuration: Network administrators manually specify both the working and recovery path through all domains. No computation needed, but doesn't scale and offers no optimization.

Head-end computation with visibility: The head-end router (or a central PCE) sees all TE information across domains and computes both diverse paths end-to-end. It then signals both paths. This is optimal but impractical for large networks with many domains.

Per-domain computation: At each domain boundary, the boundary router expands the partial path (which names only the boundary nodes of subsequent domains). This requires two variants: (1) Sequential: Working path is set up first, then recovery path is computed while excluding the resources used by the working path (using RSVP-TE Exclude Route Objects). (2) Simultaneous: Both paths are computed at each domain boundary at the same time, collecting the recovery path along with the working path's signaling messages. Simultaneous is better at avoiding trap topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways: Either administrators manually draw both routes on a map, or one central planner sees all the routes and plans both, or each company section plans its own piece while talking to the next section about how to connect.

sections.title: Schemes With Confidentiality
sections.content:
When domains (such as different service providers) need to hide internal details, the same three approaches apply, but with restricted visibility. Instead of specifying full node paths, operators specify only boundary nodes or domain identifiers, using per-domain ERO expansion.

Head-end path computation is not viable without visibility. Per-domain computation remains feasible: at each boundary, the boundary router computes a segment within its domain constraints, expanding the partial path to the next boundary. The RFC notes that, as with the non-confidential case, sequential computation may miss diverse-path solutions that simultaneous computation would find.

Inter-domain collaborative path computation offers a middle ground: domain PCEs cooperate using PCE Protocol (PCEP) extensions, exchanging path computation requests and responses without revealing full topology. An example is Backward Recursive Path Computation (BRPC), where PCEs work backward from destination to source, computing diverse segments that fit together.

The RFC emphasizes that simultaneous path computation in a collaborative scheme is more likely to find solutions when domains are multiply interconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company keeps its secrets, but when planning routes, they: let the local router plan each segment (per-domain), or have special computers at domain borders talk to each other about which paths are available (collaborative).

sections.title: Choosing the Right Approach
sections.content:
The RFC provides no single "best" scheme; the choice depends on network topology, trust relationships, and scalability needs. A single-operator multi-area network can use end-to-end computation for optimality. A multi-provider network with confidentiality needs might use collaborative per-domain computation with simultaneous path computation to balance privacy and solution quality.

Important notes: The RFC assumes domain-level routing is pre-configured (deciding which sequence of domains the paths will cross); domain re-entry (a path leaving and re-entering the same domain) is out of scope. The analysis covers end-to-end recovery, not local protection (Fast Reroute) or segment recovery, which are addressed elsewhere.

Sections 6, 7, and 8 briefly discuss topology-specific considerations (like mesh vs. linear domain connectivity), addressing considerations, and SRLG diversity (assigning shared risk groups to domains).
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the approach that matches your trust level and how many different paths exist in your network. No single approach is always best.
